Digital Marketing in Qatar: A Practical Guide for Brands Entering or Growing in the Market

by Glimpse Qatar | September 17, 2026

Qatar is a compact market, but it is not a simple one. A single campaign may need to reach Qatari nationals, long-term Arab residents, and professionals from South Asia, Europe and elsewhere, often in the same week and on the same platforms. Brands that do well here tend to make a few clear decisions early: who they are speaking to, in which language, on which channels, and at what time of year. This guide sets out those decisions in a practical order.

Start with the audience, not the channel

Arabic is Qatar's official language, and English is widely used in business. The population is largely expatriate and very international. In practice this means "people in Qatar" is rarely a useful target audience. Before you plan any activity, write down:

  • Which communities you need. Qatari nationals, Arab expatriates, Western expatriates and South Asian residents can differ in language, media habits, spending patterns and the platforms they prefer.

  • Who decides and who influences. For B2B and government-adjacent work, the person researching suppliers is often not the person who signs. Plan content for both.

  • Where they are. A restaurant in West Bay, a showroom in Lusail and a boutique at The Pearl draw on different catchments. Location should shape your targeting and your local search work.

If you have existing customer data, use it. If you are entering the market, a small research phase with real conversations is worth more than assumptions carried over from another Gulf country. A clear digital strategy at this stage saves budget later.

Plan for two languages from day one

Most brands in Qatar should operate in both Arabic and English. The common mistake is to build everything in English and translate at the end. That produces stiff Arabic copy, broken layouts and a weaker experience for the audience that often matters most.

  • Write Arabic copy as Arabic copy. Give your Arabic writer the brief, not the English text.

  • Design for right-to-left layout at the start, including forms, menus, icons with direction and email templates.

  • Decide how you will handle social channels: one bilingual account, or separate Arabic and English accounts. Either can work. What matters is consistency and enough resource to keep both languages active.

  • Have a native speaker review everything before it goes live, including captions, ad text and automated messages.

Make sure people can find you

Search is where intent shows up. Someone searching for a service in Doha is usually much closer to a decision than someone scrolling a feed.

  • Local search. Claim and complete your Google Business Profile, keep opening hours accurate (including holiday and Ramadan hours), add photos, and respond to reviews in the language they were written in.

  • Organic search. Build pages that answer the questions buyers ask in both languages. Our team covers this under SEO, including Arabic keyword research and technical setup for bilingual sites.

  • Paid search. Use search advertising to cover high-intent terms while organic visibility builds. Run separate Arabic and English campaigns so you can see what each language delivers.

Use social and paid media with a clear role for each

Social platforms are where brands in Qatar are discovered, discussed and checked. They are also where a lot of budget is wasted on content with no job to do. Give each channel one main role, such as discovery, consideration, customer care or recruitment, and measure it against that role only.

Paid social lets you target by location, language and interest, which suits a market with distinct communities. Test creative in both languages, and do not assume that the English version of an advert will perform the same way as the Arabic one. A managed social media programme should link organic content, paid support and community management so they work from one plan.

Respect the local calendar

Timing matters more in Qatar than many newcomers expect.

  • The working week runs Sunday to Thursday. Schedule B2B content, email and sales outreach around that, not around a Monday to Friday habit.

  • Ramadan and Eid move each year with the lunar calendar. Daily routines, working hours and media consumption all shift, so plan those periods separately.

  • Qatar National Day falls on 18 December, and National Sport Day is held on the second Tuesday of February. Both are moments for respectful participation, not hard selling.

  • Summer is quieter for many sectors as residents travel. Plan your bigger pushes for the cooler months unless your own data says otherwise.

Make it easy to talk to you

WhatsApp is a common business communication channel across the Gulf. Many customers would rather send a message than fill in a form or wait for an email. Add a WhatsApp option to your website and profiles, agree who answers and how quickly, and prepare replies in both languages. Treat it as a sales and service channel with the same standards as your phone line.

A simple first 90 days

  • Weeks 1 to 3: define audiences, languages and objectives. Audit your website, search presence and social profiles.

  • Weeks 4 to 6: fix the foundations. Bilingual site structure, Google Business Profile, tracking, WhatsApp and response process.

  • Weeks 7 to 10: launch always-on content and search campaigns in both languages with modest budgets.

  • Weeks 11 to 13: review results by language and audience, stop what is not working, and move budget to what is.
